module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Dickson's conjecture

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickson%27s_conjecture)
- [PrimePages glossary](https://t5k.org/glossary/xpage/DicksonsConjecture.html)
- [OEIS Wiki](https://oeis.org/wiki/Dickson%27s_conjecture)
- [MathWorld](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DicksonsConjecture.html)
- [Leonard Eugene Dickson, *History of the Theory of Numbers, Vol. I: Divisibility and Primality*](https://archive.org/details/historyoftheoryo01dickuoft)
- [Arxiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.3850)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Polynomial
namespace Dickson

/--
**Dickson's conjecture**
If a finite set of linear integer forms $f_i(n) = a_i n+b_i$ satisfies Schinzel condition,
there exist infinitely many natural numbers $m$ such that $f_i(m)$ are primes for all $i$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem dickson_conjecture (fs : Finset ℤ[X]) (hfs : ∀ f ∈ fs, f.degree = 1 ∧ BunyakovskyCondition f)
    (hfs' : SchinzelCondition fs) : Infinite {n : ℕ | ∀ f ∈ fs, (f.eval (n : ℤ)).natAbs.Prime} := by
  sorry

/-  ## Special cases -/

/--
**The generalized twin-prime conjecture**
For any positive integer $k$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p + 2k$ is prime.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem generalized_twin_primes (k : ℕ) (hk : 0 < k) :
    Infinite {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ (p + 2 * k).Prime} := by
  sorry

/--
**The infinitude of Sophie Germain primes**
There are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $2p + 1$ is prime.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_safe_primes :
    Infinite {p : ℕ | Prime p ∧ Prime (2 * p + 1)} := by
  sorry

/--
**The infinitude of cousin primes**
There are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p + 4$ is prime.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_cousin_primes :
    Infinite {p : ℕ | Prime p ∧ Prime (p + 4)} := by
  sorry

/--
**The infinitude of sexy primes**
There are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p + 6$ is prime.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_sexy_primes :
    Infinite {p : ℕ | Prime p ∧ Prime (p + 6)} := by
  sorry

/-
## Other consequences
- Landau's fourth problem (primes and perfect squares)
- Twin prime conjecture
- Artin's primitive root conjecture
- First Hardy–Littlewood conjecture

*Reference:* [Arxiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.3850)
-/

end Dickson

findings.description: The docstring at lines 39–40 omits the positive-slope assumption: it says that linear integer forms satisfying SchinzelCondition have infinitely many simultaneous prime values. The Lean correctly imposes positive leading coefficients through BunyakovskyCondition. With the ordinary positive-prime convention used by the sources, the unrestricted prose fails for f(n) = -n: {-X} satisfies SchinzelCondition (choose n = 1 for every prime), but -n is never a positive prime for n : ℕ. Both facts were verified in the scratch file. The theorem statement itself is faithful.
findings.source_evidence: Wikipedia explicitly requires each slope b_i ≥ 1. Likewise, Zhang, Notes on Dickson's Conjecture, arXiv:0906.3850v3, Introduction, states: 'f_i(x)=a_i+b_i x ... b_i≥1'. URLs: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickson%27s_conjecture and https://arxiv.org/abs/0906.3850.
findings.suggested_fix: Add 'with a_i > 0 for every i' to the docstring, using its existing coefficient convention f_i(n) = a_i n + b_i. No theorem change is needed.

reformulations.difference: The Lean uses degree-one integer polynomials satisfying BunyakovskyCondition, natural-number witnesses in SchinzelCondition, and primality of absolute values at natural inputs. The source uses positive-slope affine forms, forbids an integer greater than one dividing every product value at integer inputs, and asks for positive prime values at positive inputs.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Degree one and positive leading coefficient characterize the source's affine forms. SchinzelCondition forces their coefficients to be relatively prime, so irreducibility is redundant. A fixed divisor greater than one exists exactly when a fixed prime divisor exists; prime divisibility of a finite product reduces to divisibility of a factor. Integer witnesses can be replaced by nonnegative representatives modulo the prime. Positive slopes make every form positive beyond a common finite bound, so absolute values and the inclusion of input zero do not change infinitude. Finsets merely discard irrelevant repetitions; the empty family adds a true boundary case. Review.exact_source_reformulation in /workspace/review/scratch.lean proves the equivalence for finite sets, without sorryAx.

sources_consulted: L. E. Dickson, History of the Theory of Numbers, Vol. I, Chapter XVIII, p. 417; OCR of an alternate copy: https://archive.org/download/historyoftheoryo01dick/historyoftheoryo01dick_djvu.txt
review.notes: All five theorem statements were checked; no theorem-statement misformalization or stale status was found. Lean tests covered empty families, zero/constant polynomials, a reducible inadmissible linear polynomial, nonmonic positive linear forms, and small prime-pair examples. The OEIS Wiki reference was blocked, and the cited MathWorld and archive item URLs returned 404; the cited book was read through another scan. Separately, I could not substantiate the final informal comment's assertion that Dickson implies Landau's fourth problem: the cited arXiv introduction discusses n²+1 under Bunyakovsky, not among Dickson's consequences. That unformalized bullet deserves a citation check.
